title: How does Flink SQL handle late data in windowed aggregations — events arriving after the watermark has passed the window end are dropped by default, and you can configure allowed lateness or use side outputs at the DataStream level?
shortTitle: How does Flink SQL handle late data in windowed aggregations

s1_definition.profdef: In Flink, a windowed aggregation groups events into time windows based on event time, and a window is considered ready to fire and emit its result once the watermark passes the window's end. An event whose event-time timestamp falls inside a window but which physically arrives after the watermark has already passed that window's end is late data, and by default Flink SQL drops it, because the window has already been computed and closed. You can relax this by configuring allowed lateness, which keeps the window state alive for an extra grace period so late events update the already-emitted result, and at the lower DataStream level you can route late events to a side output to capture them for separate handling rather than losing them.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India totals the value of transactions every hour. The clock on the wall is the watermark, the bank's best estimate of how far time has progressed. At the end of each hour the bank adds up all transactions it has seen and posts the hourly total. If a transaction slip for the ten-to-eleven window turns up after the bank has already posted that hour's total, it is late. By default the bank simply ignores the straggler so the books are not reopened. But the manager can set a grace period, say fifteen extra minutes, during which a late slip still gets added and the posted total is corrected. Alternatively the bank can drop every late slip into a separate tray for manual review instead of throwing it away.
s1_definition.oneliner: Late events that miss the watermark are dropped by default in Flink SQL; allowed lateness keeps the window open for a grace period to update results, and a DataStream side output captures them instead of losing them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Flink, a windowed aggregation groups events into time windows based on event time, and a window is considered ready to fire and emit its result once the watermark passes the window's end. An event whose event-time timestamp falls inside a window but which physically arrives after the watermark has already passed that window's end is late data, and by default Flink SQL drops it, because the window has already been computed and closed. You can relax this by configuring allowed lateness, which keeps the window state alive for an extra grace period so late events update the already-emitted result, and at the lower DataStream level you can route late events to a side output to capture them for separate handling rather than losing them.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India totals the value of transactions every hour. The clock on the wall is the watermark, the bank's best estimate of how far time has progressed. At the end of each hour the bank adds up all transactions it has seen and posts the hourly total. If a transaction slip for the ten-to-eleven window turns up after the bank has already posted that hour's total, it is late. By default the bank simply ignores the straggler so the books are not reopened. But the manager can set a grace period, say fifteen extra minutes, during which a late slip still gets added and the posted total is corrected. Alternatively the bank can drop every late slip into a separate tray for manual review instead of throwing it away.

**One line to remember:** Late events that miss the watermark are dropped by default in Flink SQL; allowed lateness keeps the window open for a grace period to update results, and a DataStream side output captures them instead of losing them.

sections.s2_technical:
A windowed aggregation in Flink SQL, such as a tumbling window with `TUMBLE(TABLE txns, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' HOUR)`, assigns each event to a window by its event-time column. The watermark is Flink's assertion that no event earlier than a certain timestamp will still arrive; it is generated from the source with a bounded out-of-orderness, for example the event time minus five seconds. A window fires when the watermark reaches or passes the window end, at which point the aggregate is computed and emitted. Any event that belongs to a window whose end the watermark has already passed is late. In pure Flink SQL the default behavior is to silently drop late events, because reopening a fired window is not free and the result has already gone downstream.

Watermarks are the control knob for how much lateness you tolerate before firing. If you declare `WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL '30' SECOND`, you are telling Flink to wait thirty seconds of event time beyond a window's end before firing, which absorbs out-of-orderness up to thirty seconds; events later than that are dropped. So the first lever is simply choosing a watermark delay that matches your real-world disorder, trading latency for completeness, because a larger delay catches more stragglers but fires later. For window table-valued functions and group-window aggregations, Flink SQL also exposes a configuration, `table.exec.emit.late-fire`, together with an allowed-lateness-style setting in some window operators, so a window can keep its state for an extra period and emit an updated result when a late event arrives within that grace window, producing a retraction and a corrected row downstream.

At the DataStream level you have finer control. You call `.allowedLateness(Time.minutes(15))` on the windowed stream, which keeps each window's state for fifteen minutes past its firing so that late events within that grace period trigger a recomputation and an updated emission. You also call `.sideOutputLateData(lateTag)` to route events that are late even beyond the allowed lateness into a named side output, which you then consume as a separate stream, perhaps to write to a dead-letter table or to reconcile manually. The senior nuances are these. First, the real fix for most lateness is a correctly sized watermark, not aggressive allowed lateness, because keeping windows open costs state. Second, allowed lateness produces updates, so your sink must handle retractions or upserts, not append-only semantics. Third, side outputs guarantee you never silently lose data, which is essential in finance where a dropped transaction is a correctness and audit problem. Fourth, there is always a completeness-versus-latency trade-off: you cannot have instant results and perfect completeness at once, so you choose based on the business need, perhaps firing fast with a short watermark and reconciling late data via a side output. Understanding that watermark sizing, allowed lateness, and side outputs are three distinct tools for three distinct needs is what marks real streaming expertise.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India computes hourly transaction totals per branch for live dashboards, but mobile transactions sometimes arrive seconds or minutes after they actually occurred because of network delay. If the bank fires the hourly total the instant the clock ticks over, those delayed transactions would be dropped and the total would be slightly understated. This is exactly the late-data problem in windowed aggregation, and the first tool is a watermark delay that waits long enough to absorb normal disorder.

Problem 2 — A few transactions are so late they miss even a generous grace period, and in banking you can never silently discard a transaction. This is exactly why you use a side output: late stragglers are captured into a separate stream for reconciliation rather than lost.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models a one-hour tumbling window with a watermark delay, allowed lateness, and a side output. We define a `Txn` with an amount and an event time, a `TumblingWindowAggregator` that assigns transactions to the hourly window, fires when the watermark passes the window end, accepts late events within an allowed-lateness grace period and re-emits an updated total, and routes events late beyond the grace period to a side-output list. A `LateDataDemo` main class feeds on-time, slightly-late, and very-late transactions, advances the watermark, and prints the fired totals, the corrected totals, and the captured side-output stragglers.

The windowed SQL the demo models:

```sql
-- window_query.sql : 1-hour tumbling window, watermark absorbs 30s disorder
-- DDL: event_time TIMESTAMP(3), WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL '30' SECOND
SELECT
    window_start,
    window_end,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
    COUNT(*)    AS txn_count
FROM TABLE(
    TUMBLE(TABLE transactions, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' HOUR))
GROUP BY window_start, window_end;
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four transactions for the window from zero to one hour, with a fifteen-minute allowed lateness. T1 fifty thousand at ten minutes, T2 twelve thousand at forty minutes, T3 eight thousand at fifty-five minutes but arriving late, and T4 three thousand at fifty minutes arriving very late.

Step 1. T1 arrives on time while the window is open. Its event time of ten minutes is inside the window, so it is added. The running total is fifty thousand.

Step 2. T2 arrives on time at forty minutes, inside the window, so it is added. The total is sixty-two thousand. The window state holds both transactions and has not fired yet.

Step 3. The watermark advances to one hour, which is the window end, so the window fires. Flink emits the first result: total sixty-two thousand, count two. This is the result the dashboard sees immediately.

Step 4. T3 arrives late. Its event time of fifty-five minutes belongs to the window, but the window already fired. The current watermark, one hour ten minutes, is within the window end plus the fifteen-minute grace, so T3 is accepted as allowed-late. The total is recomputed to seventy thousand and an updated result is emitted downstream as a correction. The dashboard total is revised upward.

Step 5. T4 arrives very late. Its event time of fifty minutes belongs to the window, but the current watermark, one hour twenty minutes, is beyond the window end plus fifteen minutes of grace. T4 is therefore too late to count. Instead of being silently dropped, it is routed to the side output, where a reconciliation process can pick it up. The final in-window total stays seventy thousand, and the side output holds one straggler.

Final output:

```
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    counted on-time T1 amount=50000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    counted on-time T2 amount=12000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    FIRE window [0,3600000) total=62000 count=2
2024-01-01 00:00:00 WARNING LATE but within grace: T3 -> emit UPDATED total=70000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 SEVERE  TOO LATE -> side output T4
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    final window total = 70000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    side-output stragglers = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Flink, a windowed aggregation groups events into time windows by their event-time timestamp, and a window fires and emits its result when the watermark passes the window's end. Late data is an event that belongs to a window by its event time but physically arrives after the watermark has already passed that window's end, so the window has already been computed. The default behavior in pure Flink SQL is to drop late events, because reopening a fired window has a cost and the result has already gone downstream. The first and most important tool for handling lateness is actually the watermark itself: by declaring a watermark delay, such as event time minus thirty seconds, I tell Flink how much out-of-orderness to absorb before firing, which trades a little latency for completeness.

Beyond the watermark there are two further tools. Allowed lateness keeps a window's state alive for a grace period after it fires, so a late event arriving within that grace triggers a recomputation and emits an updated, corrected result. Because that produces an update, the sink must support retractions or upserts rather than being append-only. The second tool, available at the DataStream level, is a side output: I tag events that are late even beyond the allowed lateness and route them to a separate named stream that I consume independently, perhaps writing them to a dead-letter or reconciliation table. The senior framing is that these are three distinct levers for three needs, and that there is always a completeness-versus-latency trade-off, so I size the watermark to real disorder, use allowed lateness sparingly because open windows cost state, and rely on side outputs whenever silently losing data is unacceptable.

At the National Bank of India we computed hourly transaction totals per branch for live dashboards, and mobile transactions sometimes arrived seconds or minutes after they really happened because of network delay. I set a watermark that absorbed the normal disorder so the hourly totals were complete for the vast majority of transactions, then added a fifteen-minute allowed lateness so a straggler that still belonged to the hour corrected the posted total via an upsert rather than being lost, which the dashboard reflected as a small revision. For the rare transaction that arrived even later, I used a side output to capture it into a reconciliation table, because in banking you can never silently discard a transaction; a dropped one is both a correctness error and an audit failure. Being able to explain that late data is dropped by default, that the watermark delay is the primary control, and that allowed lateness and side outputs are the two escalation tools, with the trade-offs each carries, is exactly what shows I have built correct financial aggregations on real, out-of-order streams.
